title: Learn How to Learn
tagline: Study less, remember more: the science of learning that sticks.
description: Swap rereading and cramming for the techniques memory research rates highest: self-testing, spacing and mixing. You will build your own review schedule, protect your focus, use memory tricks that work, and get good at any new skill faster.

units.title: Why Most Studying Fails
units.description: Spot the study habits that feel productive but are not, and replace them with self-testing.

levels.title: The Illusion of Fluency
levels.summary: Why rereading and highlighting feel great and work poorly.

steps.title: Feeling ready is not being ready
steps.body:
You read your notes three times. Every line looks familiar. You feel ready.

Then the test asks you to *produce* the answer from a blank page, and it is gone.

This is the **illusion of fluency**: when material is easy to read, your brain mistakes that ease for knowing it. Recognizing something (I have seen this) is much easier than recalling it (I can bring this back on my own). Tests, jobs and real life ask for recall.
steps.tip: Before your next test, close your notes and write the five main points from memory. Whatever you cannot write is what you still need to study.

steps.prompt: Two students have the same 40 minutes for a history chapter. Ana reads it four times. Ben reads it once, then spends the rest of the time closing the book and writing down everything he can remember, checking after each try. Who will probably remember more one week later?
options: Ana, because she saw every detail four times
Ben, because pulling the facts out of memory strengthens them
They will remember about the same, since they spent equal time
Ana, because Ben made mistakes while recalling, which locks in errors
steps.explain: In a classic experiment (Roediger and Karpicke, 2006), students who studied once and then practiced recalling remembered much more a week later than students who only restudied, even though the restudy group felt more confident. Checking answers afterwards fixes the mistakes Ben makes.

steps.title: What the big review found
steps.body:
In 2013 a team of psychologists led by John Dunlosky rated ten popular study techniques using hundreds of studies.

- **High usefulness:** practice testing (quizzing yourself) and spaced practice (spreading study out over days)
- **Moderate:** explaining why a fact is true, explaining steps to yourself, mixing problem types
- **Low:** rereading, highlighting, summarizing, and a few memory tricks used alone

The two techniques students use most, rereading and highlighting, landed at the bottom.
steps.tip: Pick one class this week and swap your usual reread for a 15-minute self-quiz. Turn each heading in the chapter into a question and answer it without looking.

source.label: Dunlosky et al. (2013), Psychological Science in the Public Interest

steps.prompt: Match each study habit to how the 2013 review rated it.
pairs: Quizzing yourself with flashcards
High usefulness
Rereading the chapter
Low usefulness
Mixing different types of problems in one session
Moderate usefulness
Studying a little on several different days
High usefulness (spacing)
steps.explain: Practice testing and spacing were the only two techniques rated high. Interleaving (mixing problem types) was moderate. Rereading was rated low because it builds familiarity, not recall.

steps.prompt: If your notes look very familiar when you read them, that is good evidence you will be able to recall them on a test.
steps.explain: Familiarity is the trap. Recognizing something while looking at it is a different, easier skill than recalling it with nothing in front of you. The only honest check is to close the notes and try to produce the answer.

steps.title: Why highlighting misleads
steps.body:
Highlighting is not evil. The problem is what it replaces.

- It feels active, but you are mostly deciding *what looks important*, not practicing remembering it.
- Students often highlight too much, so nothing stands out.
- A page full of color gives a feeling of progress.

> A quick test: if you can explain an idea out loud without looking, you know it. If you can only nod along while reading, you don't yet.
steps.tip: Limit yourself to one highlight per paragraph. Then turn each highlight into a question in the margin, so the page becomes a quiz you can use later.

steps.prompt: Your friend Jordan has a chemistry test tomorrow. Jordan says: 'I'm good, I highlighted the whole chapter and reread it twice.' You want to help without sounding like a know-it-all. What do you say?

options.text: 'Nice. Want to quiz each other for 15 minutes? Cover the page and see what you can explain.'
options.feedback: Friendly and practical. It turns rereading into self-testing without lecturing, and the quiz will show Jordan which parts are actually solid.

options.text: 'Highlighting is scientifically useless. You're going to fail.'
options.feedback: Partly true about the technique, but harsh and exaggerated. Jordan will likely get defensive and ignore the advice.

options.text: 'Sounds good, you're probably ready then.'
options.feedback: Kind, but it reinforces the illusion of fluency. Jordan may discover the gaps for the first time during the test.

options.text: 'Read it a third time to be safe.'
options.feedback: More rereading mostly adds more familiarity, not more recall. The time would do more good as self-quizzing.

steps.explain: The fix for the illusion of fluency is a recall check: cover the material and try to produce it. Offering to do it together makes the advice easy to accept.

steps.prompt: Which of these are honest checks of whether you actually know something? Select all that apply.
steps.hint: Ask of each option: do you have to produce the answer yourself, or is it sitting in front of you?
options: Explaining the idea out loud to someone without notes
Rereading your notes and feeling that they make sense
Writing everything you remember on a blank page, then checking
Doing practice problems without looking at the worked examples
Recognizing the right answer in your textbook's bold words
steps.explain: Recall checks make you produce the answer with nothing in front of you. Rereading and recognizing bold terms only test familiarity.

steps.prompt: Think of the next test, exam or thing you need to learn. Which low-value habit (rereading, highlighting, copying notes) will you swap for a recall check this week, and when?
steps.placeholder: e.g. Tuesday after dinner: instead of rereading bio notes, I'll do a blank-page recall for 10 minutes...

levels.title: Retrieval Practice
levels.summary: The single most reliable study technique, and four easy ways to use it.

steps.title: Pulling, not pushing
steps.body:
Most study tries to *push* information into your head. Memory research says the bigger gains come from *pulling* it back out.

Each time you successfully recall something, the memory gets stronger and easier to find next time. This is called **retrieval practice** or the **testing effect**. The test is not just a measurement; it is the workout.

It works for facts, concepts, vocabulary, procedures, and across ages from kids to adults.
steps.tip: End every study session with three minutes of recall: close everything and say or write what you just learned. Then open the notes and check.

steps.prompt: Which of these count as retrieval practice? Select all that apply.
options: Flashcards where you say the answer before flipping
Flashcards where you flip right away and read both sides
Answering end-of-chapter questions before checking the book
Copying your notes neatly into a new notebook
Teaching the topic to a sibling from memory
steps.explain: Retrieval means you produce the answer first. Flipping a card instantly, or copying notes, lets you skip the effort of recalling, so you lose most of the benefit.

steps.title: Four ways to self-test
steps.body:
- **Blank page:** write everything you remember about a topic, then check and fill the gaps in a different color.
- **Flashcards:** question on one side, answer on the other. Say or write the answer before flipping.
- **Practice questions:** use old tests, textbook questions, or turn headings into questions.
- **Teach it:** explain it out loud to someone (or an empty chair) without notes.

Always check your answer afterward. Feedback fixes errors so they do not stick.
steps.tip: When you finish a chapter, write five questions on an index card before you put the book away. Answer them the next morning before breakfast.

steps.prompt: Put the blank-page method in the right order.
items: Study the material once carefully
Close the book and put away notes
Write down everything you can remember
Open the notes and check what you got right and wrong
Add the missing parts in a different color
Repeat on another day, focusing on the colored parts
steps.explain: Study, close, recall, check, fill gaps, then come back later. The colored parts show exactly where to spend your next session.

steps.prompt: Getting answers wrong during practice hurts your learning, so you should only quiz yourself once you are sure you know the material.
steps.hint: Think about what happens right after you get a practice answer wrong and then check it.
steps.explain: Trying to recall, even unsuccessfully, followed by checking the right answer, helps learning. Researchers have even found that taking a test before studying a topic (a pretest) can improve later learning. Waiting until you feel sure just delays the useful struggle.

steps.title: Make it a little hard
steps.body:
The best practice feels slightly uncomfortable. Psychologist Robert Bjork calls these **desirable difficulties**: effort that slows you down now but makes memory last.

Signs you are doing it right:
- You have to pause and think before answering.
- You get some wrong, then fix them.
- It feels slower than rereading.

If every answer pops out instantly, the material is learned for now. Move on, and test it again in a few days.

source.label: Bjork and Bjork (2011), Making things hard on yourself, but in a good way

steps.tip: If a flashcard pops into your head instantly three times in a row, take it out of today's pile. Spend your minutes on the cards that make you pause.

steps.prompt: You have 2 hours tonight for a biology test on Friday covering 3 chapters. Which plan uses retrieval practice best?

options.text: Skim each chapter once (40 min), then spend 80 min answering practice questions and doing blank-page recall, checking after each round.
options.feedback: Strong plan. A quick review gives you material to work with, and most of the time goes to recall with feedback.

options.text: Reread all three chapters carefully, highlighting key terms.
options.feedback: This will feel productive but mostly builds familiarity. You will not find out what you cannot recall until the test.

options.text: Rewrite your class notes neatly so they are easier to read later.
options.feedback: Neat notes are nice, but copying is not recall. It is a low-value use of two hours.

options.text: Do practice questions with the answer key open next to you so you do not waste time being stuck.
options.feedback: Peeking turns recall into recognition. Try first, then check.

steps.explain: Spend most study time producing answers from memory, with feedback after each attempt. A short initial review is fine, but it should not take most of the time.

steps.prompt: You turn a textbook heading into a question. The heading is 'Causes of the French Revolution.' Which flashcard is the best retrieval prompt?
steps.hint: A good retrieval prompt makes you produce the answer. Which card can you not answer just by reading it?
options: Front: 'French Revolution' / Back: the whole page of notes
Front: 'Name three causes of the French Revolution and explain one' / Back: the causes and a short explanation
Front: 'Did the French Revolution have causes?' / Back: 'Yes'
Front: the causes / Back: 'French Revolution'
steps.explain: A good card asks a specific question that makes you produce real content. Too broad (a whole page) is hard to check, too easy (yes/no) tests nothing, and showing the answer on the front gives it away.

steps.prompt: Pick one class or skill. Write five questions you could quiz yourself with this week, and when you will do it.
steps.placeholder: 1. What are the three ... ? 2. Why does ... ? I'll quiz myself Thursday on the bus.

levels.title: Learning Myths to Drop
levels.summary: Learning styles, the 10% brain, and other ideas that waste your time.

steps.title: Popular but wrong
steps.body:
Some ideas about learning are repeated so often they feel like facts. Believing them can steer you toward weaker study methods, or make you think you are just 'not a math person.'

In this level you will test yourself on common myths. For each, ask: *What is the evidence? Who checked it?*

steps.prompt: People learn best when teaching matches their learning style (visual, auditory, or kinesthetic).
steps.explain: People do have preferences, but a major 2008 review found no good evidence that matching teaching to a preferred style improves learning. What works is matching the method to the *content*: maps for geography, audio for pronunciation, hands-on for a skill like welding.

steps.title: The learning styles myth
steps.body:
To prove learning styles, you would need an experiment where visual learners do better with pictures *and* auditory learners do better with audio. Researchers looking for that pattern found it almost nowhere, and several studies found the opposite.

The practical problem: if you label yourself a 'visual learner,' you may skip the things that work for everyone, like self-testing and spacing.

> Combining words and pictures helps almost everyone. That is not a style; it is just good teaching.
steps.tip: When you study, pair words with a quick sketch: a timeline, a labeled diagram or a flow chart. Words plus pictures help almost everyone, whatever 'style' a quiz gave you.

source.label: Pashler et al. (2008), Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence

steps.prompt: Humans only use about 10% of their brains, so you could unlock much more with the right training.
steps.explain: Brain scans show activity across virtually all brain regions over the course of a day, and damage to almost any area causes some problem. The 10% claim has no scientific basis.

steps.prompt: Taking lecture notes by hand instead of on a laptop has been reliably shown to double how much you learn.
steps.hint: Look closely at the strength of the claim. What would 'reliably double' require research to show?
steps.explain: A famous 2014 study suggested a handwriting advantage, but larger replications found small or no reliable difference. What matters more: putting ideas in your own words instead of transcribing, and not getting distracted by other tabs on the laptop.

steps.title: What is true about ability
steps.body:
- Your brain changes with practice. Skills and knowledge grow with effort and good methods.
- People do differ in starting points and speed, so comparing yourself to others is often misleading.
- 'I'm not a math person' usually means 'I haven't practiced math with good methods yet.'

Be careful with hype in the other direction too: short 'growth mindset' pep talks have small average effects in studies. Belief helps you start. Method and practice do the work.

source.label: Sisk et al. (2018), Psychological Science: two meta-analyses on growth mindset

steps.tip: Next time you think 'I'm not good at this,' finish the sentence with 'yet' and name one method to try, such as ten practice problems with the answer key.

steps.prompt: Match each myth to what the evidence actually shows.
pairs: Learning styles
Match the method to the content, not to a personal style
10% of the brain
Virtually all of the brain is active over a day
Handwriting doubles learning
Replications found little or no reliable difference
Rereading is the safest way to study
It builds familiarity, not reliable recall
steps.explain: Each myth sounds plausible, which is why it spreads. The better habit is asking what kind of study tested the claim.

steps.prompt: Your younger cousin took an online quiz that said she is a 'kinesthetic learner,' so she says reading and flashcards are pointless for her. She has a vocabulary test next week. What do you tell her?

options.text: 'Lots of people believe that, but studies did not find that matching a style helps. Flashcards work for nearly everyone. Want to make some and quiz each other while walking around?'
options.feedback: Corrects the myth gently, recommends what works, and even lets her move while practicing, which may make it more enjoyable without pretending it is the key.

options.text: 'Then build models of the words with clay instead. That's your style.'
options.feedback: This follows the myth and costs her time. Clay models are slow and do not practice recalling meanings.

options.text: 'Learning styles are fake, so you're just lazy.'
options.feedback: Corrects the myth but insults her. She is likely to tune you out.

options.text: 'The quiz is probably right; everyone is different.'
options.feedback: People differ in many ways, but this particular claim is not supported. Agreeing steers her away from methods that work.

steps.explain: Correct a myth kindly, then replace it with something useful. Here, self-testing with flashcards is the evidence-based method.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Matching lessons to a learning style does not improve learning. Use self-testing and spacing whatever your preferences.
- You use all of your brain.
- Laptop or paper matters less than processing ideas in your own words.
- When you hear a learning 'fact,' ask: what study showed that, and has anyone repeated it?

**This week:** if you catch yourself saying 'I'm just not a ___ person,' replace it with 'I haven't practiced ___ the right way yet' and plan one self-test session.

units.title: Make It Stick
units.description: Use spacing and mixing to make memories last for months, and build your own review schedule.

levels.title: The Spacing Effect
levels.summary: Why the same hours spread out beat one big cram session.

steps.title: Forgetting is normal
steps.body:
Right after you learn something, you start forgetting it, fast at first and then slower. Psychologists have measured this **forgetting curve** since the 1880s.

The good news: every time you review just as a memory is starting to fade, the curve gets flatter. The memory lasts longer before the next drop.

Cramming puts all your reviews in one night. You feel ready the next morning, but most of it is gone weeks later.

source.label: Murre and Dros (2015), Replication of Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve, PLOS ONE

steps.tip: Start reviewing for your next big test a week early. Do three short self-tests on different days instead of one long session the night before.

steps.prompt: Maya and Leo each study Spanish vocab for 3 hours total. Maya does 3 hours on Sunday night before Monday's quiz. Leo does 30 minutes a day for six days. Which statement is most likely true?
options: Maya does better on Monday and much better a month later
Leo does about as well or better on Monday and much better a month later
They do the same both times because total time is equal
Leo does worse on both because his sessions were too short
steps.explain: Cramming can work okay for a test the next day, but spaced study gives similar or better short-term results and far better long-term memory. Total time is the same; the timing is what differs.

steps.title: How far apart?
steps.body:
A big 2008 study taught over 1,350 people facts, then reviewed them after different gaps and tested them up to a year later.

The best gap depended on how long you need to remember:
- Need it in about a week: a gap of roughly **20 to 40%** of that time worked best (1 to 3 days).
- Need it for a year: a gap of about **5 to 10%** (a few weeks).

For tests a few weeks to a couple of months away, a gap of about **20%** of the time is a good middle-ground rule of thumb.

Too short a gap wastes the review. Too long and you have forgotten too much. A simple rule: **review after a few days, then after a week or two.**
steps.tip: For a test in about two weeks, put two 15-minute reviews in your calendar, a few days apart. Set reminders so the spacing happens without you having to remember.

steps.prompt: Your final exam is 30 days away. Using the rule of thumb of a review gap about 20% of the time until the test, how many days should you wait between your first study session and your first review?
steps.hint: Find 20% of the 30 days. Turning 20% into a fraction (one fifth) makes it quick.
steps.explain: 20% of 30 days = 0.20 x 30 = 6 days. That is a starting point, not a law: a day or two either way is fine. What matters is spreading the reviews out instead of cramming.

steps.prompt: Spaced study usually feels harder than cramming, even though it works better.
steps.explain: When you come back after a gap, some of the material has faded, so recalling it takes effort. That effort is exactly what strengthens memory. Cramming feels smoother because everything is still fresh, which is the illusion of fluency again.

steps.title: Spacing + testing = the power combo
steps.body:
Spacing and retrieval practice work best together. Each spaced session should be a **self-test**, not a reread.

A simple week for one class:
- **Day 1:** learn the new material, do a quick self-test
- **Day 3:** blank-page recall, fix gaps
- **Day 7:** practice questions mixing this week's and last week's topics

Ten to twenty minutes per session is plenty.
steps.tip: Make a weekly review slot for each class, like 'Sunday 7 p.m.: 15-minute mixed quiz on this week's and last week's notes.' Put it in your phone calendar on repeat.

steps.prompt: It is Monday. You have a driver's permit test on Saturday and about 2 hours total you can spend on the handbook. What is the best plan?

options.text: Read the key sections Monday, then do 20-30 minute practice quizzes on Tuesday, Thursday and Friday, focusing on questions you missed.
options.feedback: This spreads practice across the week and uses testing each time. The questions you miss tell you where to focus.

options.text: Do all 2 hours Friday night so it is fresh for Saturday.
options.feedback: This can get you through Saturday, but it feels riskier and you will forget the rules faster, even though you need them for real driving.

options.text: Read the handbook for 2 hours on Monday and then relax the rest of the week.
options.feedback: One session, early, with no review: most of it will fade by Saturday.

options.text: Read one page every day without quizzing yourself.
options.feedback: Spaced, but rereading only. Add self-tests to get the real benefit.

steps.explain: Spread sessions out and make each one a self-test. Spacing alone helps, testing alone helps, both together help most.

steps.prompt: Order these study plans from least effective to most effective for remembering material a month from now.
steps.hint: Two things matter: is the time spread over days, and does each session test you or just show you the material?
items: Reread everything once the night before
Reread everything on three different days
Quiz yourself once the night before
Quiz yourself on three different days
steps.explain: Single rereading is weakest. Spacing improves rereading. Testing beats rereading. Testing on spaced days combines both of the highest-rated techniques.

steps.prompt: Look at your calendar. For one thing you need to remember (a test, a language, work training), write down three spaced review days for the next two weeks.
steps.placeholder: e.g. Learn on Mon, review Wed, review next Mon, mixed quiz the Friday after...

levels.title: Build a Review Schedule
levels.summary: Set up flashcard boxes or an app so the right cards come back at the right time.

steps.title: Let the system decide
steps.body:
Spacing by hand gets messy once you have hundreds of facts. A **spaced repetition system** decides what to review each day:

- Cards you get right come back later and later.
- Cards you miss come back soon.

You spend your time on what you don't know yet, instead of re-reviewing what you already do. You can do it with paper (the Leitner box) or with a free app such as Anki.
steps.tip: Download a free spaced repetition app like Anki tonight and make ten cards for one class. Review whatever it shows you each day for one week.

steps.title: The Leitner box (paper version)
steps.body:
Get index cards and 3 envelopes or boxes.

- **Box 1:** review every day
- **Box 2:** review every 3 days
- **Box 3:** review once a week

All new cards start in Box 1. Answer correctly (out loud, before flipping) and the card moves up one box. Get it wrong and it goes **back to Box 1**, no matter where it was.

Within a couple of weeks the easy cards drift to Box 3 and your daily time goes to the hard ones.
steps.tip: Grab three envelopes, label them 'Daily,' 'Every 3 days' and 'Weekly,' and start a Leitner box for one subject with 20 index cards this week.

steps.prompt: A card about the Krebs cycle is in Box 3. On your weekly review you get it wrong. Where does it go?
options: It stays in Box 3 and you try again next week
It moves to Box 2
It goes back to Box 1
You throw it out because it is too hard
steps.explain: In the Leitner system a missed card restarts in Box 1 so you see it daily until it sticks again. A hard card deserves more practice, not less.

steps.prompt: You use expanding review gaps: first review 1 day after learning, then 3 days after that, then 7 days after that, then 14 days after that. You learn a set of cards on day 0. On what day number is the fourth review?
steps.hint: Start at day 0 and add each gap in turn: 1, then 3, then 7, then 14. Keep a running total.
steps.explain: Add the gaps: day 0 + 1 = day 1, + 3 = day 4, + 7 = day 11, + 14 = day 25. Expanding gaps let you review less and less often as the memory strengthens.

steps.title: Using an app well
steps.body:
Apps like Anki schedule cards for you. Three rules that matter more than settings:

- **Make your own cards** (or edit shared ones). Writing them is part of learning.
- **One idea per card.** 'What does mitochondria do?' beats a card with five facts.
- **Review daily, even 10 minutes.** Skipping days piles up reviews.

Be honest when grading yourself. Marking a near-miss as 'correct' just hides it from you.
steps.tip: In your flashcard app, set a daily limit of about 10 new cards. Small, steady additions keep your daily reviews short enough that you actually do them.

steps.prompt: Which of these are well-made flashcards? Select all that apply.
options: Front: 'What year did the US Constitution take effect?' Back: '1789'
Front: 'World War I' Back: a full page of causes, battles, dates and results
Front: 'Spanish: la biblioteca' Back: 'library (not bookstore = la libreria)'
Front: 'Why does ice float?' Back: 'It is less dense than liquid water because its molecules form an open crystal'
Front: 'Everything about photosynthesis' Back: textbook pages 112-118
steps.explain: Good cards ask one clear question with a short answer you can check. Cards that point to a whole topic or page can't be graded honestly and turn into rereading.

steps.prompt: You started using a flashcard app for a language. After a busy week you open it and see 340 cards due. What do you do?
steps.hint: Think about what you can realistically finish today, and how to keep the pile from growing again tomorrow.

options.text: Do reviews in 15-minute chunks over the next few days, pause adding new cards until the pile is under control, then restart daily.
options.feedback: Realistic and sustainable. Clearing the backlog first protects the cards you already learned.

options.text: Delete the deck and start over.
options.feedback: Many of those cards are partly learned. Deleting throws that progress away.

options.text: Mark them all as 'easy' to make the number go away.
options.feedback: The app will push them far into the future, and you will have forgotten them by then. You are fooling the schedule, not learning.

options.text: Keep adding 30 new cards a day and ignore the old ones.
options.feedback: The backlog will keep growing, and older cards will decay.

steps.explain: Spaced repetition works when it is a small daily habit. After a gap, clear the backlog in chunks and pause new cards instead of quitting or cheating the system.

steps.prompt: Set up a spaced repetition routine in the right order.
items: Pick one subject you need to remember for weeks or longer
Write 10-20 cards, one idea each
Pick a fixed daily time (e.g. after breakfast)
Review due cards, answering before you flip
Add a few new cards only after reviews are done
steps.explain: Choose the subject, make good cards, attach the habit to a fixed time, and always do reviews before adding new material.

steps.prompt: Make 10 flashcards for something you need to learn this month (paper or app). Where and when will you do your daily review?
steps.placeholder: e.g. 10 Spanish verbs in Anki, review on the bus at 7:40 each morning...

levels.title: Mix It Up: Interleaving
levels.summary: Practicing different kinds of problems together teaches you when to use each one.

steps.title: Blocked vs mixed
steps.body:
Most textbooks give you 20 problems of the same type in a row. That is **blocked practice**: AAAA, BBBB, CCCC.

**Interleaved practice** mixes them: A, C, B, A, B, C.

Blocked feels smooth, because you know which method to use before you read the problem. But on a real test, problems don't come labeled. Interleaving forces you to practice the hardest part: **figuring out which method fits.**

source.label: Rohrer, Dedrick and Burgess (2014), Psychonomic Bulletin and Review, via What Works Clearinghouse

steps.tip: On your next math homework, do the problems in a shuffled order, or add three problems from an earlier chapter, so you practice choosing the method.

steps.prompt: In one study, 7th graders practiced math either blocked or interleaved. On a surprise test two weeks later, the interleaved group averaged 72% and the blocked group averaged 38%. How many percentage points higher was the interleaved group?
steps.hint: Subtract the blocked group's score from the interleaved group's score.
steps.explain: 72 - 38 = 34 percentage points. That is almost double the score from the same practice problems, just arranged differently.

steps.title: It feels worse but works better
steps.body:
In a study where people learned to recognize painters' styles, those who saw the paintings mixed together identified new paintings better. Yet most people still rated seeing one artist at a time as the better method.

That gap between feeling and result is why so few students interleave on their own.

**Where it helps most:** things that are easy to confuse, such as math problem types, similar words in a language, types of chemical reactions, or plays in a sport.
steps.tip: Make one flashcard deck that mixes words you keep confusing, like similar Spanish verbs or similar chemical reactions, and review them together.

steps.prompt: Match each practice plan to its type.
pairs: 20 area-of-circle problems, then 20 area-of-triangle problems
Blocked
Circle, triangle, rectangle, triangle, circle problems shuffled
Interleaved
Basketball: 50 free throws, then 50 layups
Blocked (fine for first learning a move)
Spanish: mixed quiz of ser vs estar sentences
Interleaved (great for easily confused items)
steps.explain: Blocked practice can help when a skill is brand new. Once you know the basics of each type, mixing them builds the skill of choosing correctly.

steps.prompt: Interleaving means you should switch between completely unrelated subjects, like history and math, every few minutes.
steps.hint: Reread what interleaving mixes: types of problems you might confuse, or anything at all?
steps.explain: Interleaving helps by mixing things that could be confused within one skill area (different problem types in math, similar words in a language). Jumping between unrelated subjects every few minutes just adds switching costs.

steps.prompt: Your algebra homework has 30 problems all about factoring. The unit test will cover factoring, the quadratic formula and completing the square. You finished the homework easily. How do you study for the test?

options.text: Make a mixed set: pick 4-5 problems from each section, shuffle them, and for each one decide which method to use before solving.
options.feedback: This practices exactly what the test demands: recognizing the problem type and picking the method.

options.text: Redo the 30 factoring problems since you know those best.
options.feedback: Comfortable, but it skips two topics and never practices choosing between methods.

options.text: Do 20 quadratic formula problems, then 20 completing the square problems.
options.feedback: Better than nothing, but still blocked. On the test the problems will not come sorted.

options.text: Read the worked examples in each section.
options.feedback: Reading examples is passive. You need to try problems yourself.

steps.explain: Once you know each method, mix them. Deciding which tool to use is a skill that blocked practice never trains.

steps.title: How to interleave this week
steps.body:
- **Math or science:** after finishing a chapter, do mixed review sets that include older chapters.
- **Languages:** mix vocabulary from different units in one flashcard deck.
- **Sports and music:** once you know each move or piece, practice them in random order instead of repeating one for 30 minutes.
- **Flashcard apps** already mix cards for you.

Expect it to feel clumsier. That is the sign it is working.
steps.tip: At practice, once you know your drills, ask a friend to call them out in random order instead of repeating one move for half an hour.

steps.prompt: Which statement about interleaving is accurate?
options: It helps most when the things being mixed are easy to confuse with each other
It makes practice feel easier and faster
It replaces the need for spacing
It only works for math
steps.explain: Interleaving trains you to tell similar things apart. It tends to feel harder, it combines well with spacing (mixing naturally spreads each topic out), and it has worked in math, art, science and motor skills.

steps.prompt: Pick one subject or skill. Write a short mixed practice set for this week: which 3 types of problems or moves will you shuffle together?
steps.placeholder: e.g. Chemistry: balancing equations + mole conversions + limiting reagent, 4 of each, shuffled...

units.title: Focus, Notes and Memory Tricks
units.description: Protect your attention, take notes you can actually study from, and memorize lists with ease.

levels.title: Deep Focus
levels.summary: Why switching tasks costs more than you think, and how to set up a focus block.

steps.title: There is no real multitasking
steps.body:
When you text while studying, your brain is not doing both at once. It is **switching** back and forth, and every switch has a cost: a moment to reload what you were doing.

Worse, part of your attention stays stuck on the last thing. Researcher Sophie Leroy calls this **attention residue**. After checking a message, your mind keeps half-thinking about it for a while.

A few quick checks can quietly eat a big part of an hour of study.

source.label: Leroy (2009), Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

steps.tip: Turn on Do Not Disturb or a Focus mode during homework, and allow calls only from family. You stop paying the restart cost of every buzz.

steps.prompt: Suppose each phone check takes 1 minute, plus about 2 more minutes before you are fully focused again. You check 4 times in a 30-minute study block. How many minutes of full focus are left in that block?
steps.hint: Find the cost of one check (the check plus the refocus time). Multiply by the number of checks, then subtract from 30.
steps.explain: Each check costs 1 + 2 = 3 minutes. 4 checks x 3 = 12 minutes lost. 30 - 12 = 18 minutes of real focus. (These are example numbers; the exact refocus time varies by person and task.)

steps.title: Set up a focus block
steps.body:
1. **Pick one task** with a clear finish: 'Do problems 1-15,' not 'study chem.'
2. **Phone out of reach**, ideally in another room. Notifications off.
3. **Set a timer** for 25-50 minutes.
4. **Keep a distraction note**: when a thought pops up ('reply to Sam'), write it down and keep going.
5. **Take a real break** of 5-10 minutes: stand up, move, drink water. Not scrolling.

The 25-minute version is often called the Pomodoro technique.
steps.tip: Keep a sticky note next to you while you study. When a thought like 'text Sam' pops up, write it down and keep working. Handle the list on your break.

steps.prompt: Put these focus block steps in order.
items: Choose one specific task with a clear finish line
Put your phone in another room and close extra tabs
Start a 25-50 minute timer
Write down distracting thoughts instead of acting on them
Take a 5-10 minute movement break when the timer ends
steps.explain: Decide, remove distractions, time it, park stray thoughts, then rest. The break matters: it makes the next block easier to start.

steps.prompt: Keeping your phone face-down on the desk is just as good as putting it in another room, as long as you don't touch it.
steps.hint: Is a phone in sight a distraction only when you touch it?
steps.explain: Studies on whether a nearby phone drains attention have been mixed, but the practical point is simple: a phone within reach makes checking a one-second decision. Out of the room, you have to get up first, and most urges pass before you do.

steps.prompt: You have an essay due Friday. You sit down Wednesday night and your group chat keeps buzzing about weekend plans. What is the best move?

options.text: Text the group 'Doing homework till 9, will catch up after,' turn on Do Not Disturb, and leave the phone in the kitchen.
options.feedback: You let friends know so you won't worry about missing something, then remove the temptation. After 9 you get the plans without the guilt.

options.text: Keep the chat open and reply quickly between paragraphs.
options.feedback: Every reply is a switch plus attention residue. The essay will take much longer and be worse.

options.text: Mute the chat but keep the phone next to you in case something important happens.
options.feedback: Better than nothing, but the phone in reach still pulls at you. Real emergencies usually come as calls, which you can allow through Do Not Disturb settings.

options.text: Give up on the essay tonight and do it all Thursday.
options.feedback: That shrinks your time and adds stress. The distraction problem will still be there Thursday.

steps.explain: Make focus easy: tell people you are unavailable, block notifications, and put physical distance between you and the phone.

steps.title: Build focus like a muscle
steps.body:
If 50 minutes of focus sounds impossible, start smaller. Twenty minutes of true focus beats an hour of half-focus.

- Week 1: two 20-minute blocks a day
- Week 2: two 30-minute blocks
- Later: 45-50 minute blocks for hard work

Your hardest task goes in your best time of day. For many people that is the morning; for some teens it is later. Track when you focus best and protect that time.
steps.tip: For one week, note the time of day each study session felt easiest. Then put your hardest subject in that slot next week.

steps.prompt: Which of these is the best break between two focus blocks?
options: Scrolling short videos for 10 minutes
Walking around, getting water, and stretching for 5-10 minutes
Starting a different homework assignment
Checking every notification you missed
steps.explain: A break should let your attention rest. Short videos and notification catch-up start new threads of attention residue and often stretch far past 10 minutes.

steps.prompt: Plan two focus blocks for this week: what task, what day and time, and where your phone will be.
steps.placeholder: e.g. Tue 4:00-4:30 math set 3, phone charging in the kitchen...

levels.title: Notes That Work
levels.summary: Take notes you can study from by turning them into questions.

steps.title: Notes are a tool, not a transcript
steps.body:
Many students try to write down everything a teacher says. That turns you into a slow recording device, and you are not thinking about the ideas.

Good notes do two jobs:
- **During class:** make you process the ideas by putting them in your own words.
- **After class:** give you something to **quiz yourself** from.

Notes you only reread are a weak study tool. Notes you test yourself on are a strong one.
steps.tip: In your next class, write ideas in your own short phrases instead of copying sentences. If you cannot reword it, write a question mark to ask about later.

steps.title: The Cornell method
steps.body:
Draw a line down your page about a third of the way from the left. Leave space at the bottom.

- **Right side (during class):** main ideas and examples, in your own words, short phrases.
- **Left side (after class, same day):** write **questions** that the notes answer. 'What are the 3 branches of government?'
- **Bottom:** a 2-3 sentence summary.

To study: cover the right side, read each question on the left, and answer from memory. Your notes just became flashcards.
steps.tip: Tonight, draw a Cornell line on one page of today's notes and write three questions in the left column. Cover the right side tomorrow and answer them.

steps.prompt: Put the Cornell notes routine in order.
items: Split the page: narrow question column, wide notes column, summary space
During class, write key ideas in your own words on the right
Later that day, write questions in the left column
Write a short summary at the bottom
To study, cover the right side and answer each question from memory
steps.explain: Set up, capture, turn into questions, summarize, then self-test. The questions are what turn notes into retrieval practice.

steps.prompt: Your teacher says: 'Mitochondria convert energy from food into ATP, which cells use to power almost everything they do.' Which note is best?
steps.hint: The best note is short, uses your own words, and keeps the key idea. Which one could you quiz yourself from?
options: Mitochondria convert energy from food into ATP, which cells use to power almost everything they do.
Mito = power plant: food energy -> ATP (cell's energy currency)
Mitochondria
ATP!!!
steps.explain: The second note is short, in your own words, and keeps the key relationship (food energy becomes ATP). Copying word for word skips processing; a single word loses the meaning.

steps.prompt: Going over your notes the same day, even for 10 minutes, and turning them into questions helps more than waiting until the night before the test.
steps.explain: A quick same-day pass catches confusing parts while you still remember the lesson, and writing questions starts your retrieval practice early. It also spaces out your studying.

steps.prompt: In a fast lecture, you can't keep up and your notes are a mess of half-sentences. What is the best fix?

options.text: Write fewer, shorter notes on the main ideas during class, then spend 10 minutes that evening filling gaps from the slides or textbook and adding questions.
options.feedback: This keeps your attention on understanding during class and moves the cleanup to a quick review that also strengthens memory.

options.text: Record the lecture and transcribe the whole thing later.
options.feedback: Transcribing is very slow and mostly copying. A recording is fine for checking a confusing part, not for rewriting everything.

options.text: Stop taking notes and just listen.
options.feedback: Listening matters, but with no notes you have nothing to quiz yourself from later.

options.text: Ask a friend for their notes and skip your own.
options.feedback: Comparing notes can help, but writing your own forces you to process the ideas, which is a big part of the value.

steps.explain: Capture key ideas briefly during class, then do a short same-day review that fills gaps and turns notes into questions.

steps.prompt: Which habits make notes more useful for studying? Select all that apply.
options: Writing ideas in your own words
Copying every slide word for word
Adding questions you could be tested on
Drawing simple diagrams that show how ideas connect
Using five highlighter colors on every page
steps.explain: Own words, questions and simple diagrams make you think about meaning and set up self-testing. Copying and heavy highlighting look busy but do little.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Write short notes in your own words. Don't transcribe.
- Same day: add questions in a side column and a short summary.
- Study by covering your notes and answering the questions.
- Laptop or paper both work; if you use a laptop, close every other tab.

**This week:** use the Cornell layout for one class or meeting and quiz yourself from it within 24 hours.

levels.title: Memory Tricks That Work
levels.summary: Chunking, the memory palace and mnemonics for lists, names and numbers.

steps.title: Your mental workbench is small
steps.body:
**Working memory** is the part of your mind that holds things while you use them, like a phone number you are about to type. It is tiny: current research suggests about **4 chunks** at once.

The trick is making each chunk bigger. 1-7-7-6 is four items. **1776** (the year of the Declaration of Independence) is one chunk.

Experts are not born with bigger working memories. They have learned patterns that pack lots of information into one chunk.

source.label: Cowan (2010), The Magical Mystery Four, Current Directions in Psychological Science

steps.tip: When you need to remember a code, a list or a phone number, split it into groups of three or four before you try to hold it in your head.

steps.prompt: The phone number 8015551234 has 10 digits. If you chunk it the usual way (801-555-1234), how many chunks must you hold in working memory?
steps.hint: Count the groups, not the digits. How many pieces does the dashed version split the number into?
steps.explain: 801, 555 and 1234: three chunks instead of ten separate digits. That is why phone numbers and card numbers are printed in groups.

steps.title: The memory palace
steps.body:
Pick a place you know well, like your home. Walk a fixed route: front door, couch, kitchen sink, fridge, your bed.

To remember a list, place a vivid, weird image of each item at each stop. Groceries: eggs smashed on the front door, milk flooding the couch, bananas clogging the sink.

To recall, mentally walk the route. In a 2017 study, beginners who trained this way for about 6 weeks went from recalling about 26 words of a 72-word list to about 62, and still remembered far more months later.
steps.tip: Next time you shop without a list, place each item along your route home: front door, couch, sink. Walk the route in your head at the store.

steps.prompt: Put the steps for using a memory palace in order.
items: Choose a familiar place and fix a route with clear stops
Make a vivid, unusual image for each item on your list
Place each image at the next stop along the route
Recall by mentally walking the route in order
Rehearse the walk again later to make it stick
steps.explain: Familiar route, vivid images, place them in order, walk it back, and review it later. Spacing still helps memory tricks.

steps.prompt: Match each memory technique to the job it does best.
pairs: Chunking
Long strings of digits or letters
Memory palace
An ordered list, like speech points
Acronym (e.g. HOMES for the Great Lakes)
A short fixed set of names
Retrieval practice with spacing
Understanding and keeping a whole subject
steps.explain: Memory tricks are great for lists and arbitrary facts. For understanding a subject, testing and spacing still do the heavy lifting.

steps.prompt: Memory tricks like acronyms can replace understanding: if you memorize the mnemonic, you know the topic.
steps.hint: An acronym tells you what the items are called. Does it tell you what they mean?
steps.explain: A mnemonic helps you retrieve a list, but not why the items matter or how they connect. In the 2013 review, mnemonic tricks used alone were rated low for learning whole subjects. Use them for lists, then practice explaining the ideas.

steps.prompt: You are giving a 5-minute class presentation without notes and need to remember your 5 main points in order. What is a smart way to prepare?

options.text: Assign each point to a stop in your house with a vivid image, then rehearse walking the route and saying each point out loud on a few different days.
options.feedback: A memory palace locks in the order, and spaced out-loud rehearsal is retrieval practice for the content.

options.text: Read the script over and over the night before.
options.feedback: Rereading builds familiarity, not recall. You may blank under pressure.

options.text: Write the points on your hand.
options.feedback: That might work in a pinch but does not build memory, and it may not be allowed.

options.text: Memorize the whole speech word for word.
options.feedback: Very slow, and if you lose one word you can lose your place. Remembering points and speaking naturally is safer.

steps.explain: Use a memory trick for the order and practice saying the content out loud for the substance.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Working memory holds about 4 chunks. Group information to fit more in.
- A memory palace links items to places along a route you know. Beginners can get large gains with practice.
- Acronyms and silly sentences work for short fixed lists.
- Memory tricks help you find information; understanding still comes from explaining and self-testing.

**This week:** build a 5-stop memory palace for something real: a shopping list, speech points or the steps of a process.

units.title: Learn Any Skill Faster
units.description: Practice with purpose, get fast feedback, and use sleep to lock in what you learn.

levels.title: Deliberate Practice
levels.summary: Why hours alone do not make you good, and what kind of practice does.

steps.title: Practice is not just repetition
steps.body:
Someone who has driven for 20 years is not a race car driver. Someone who has played guitar for 5 years by strumming the same 4 songs may barely improve.

Psychologist Anders Ericsson studied experts and described **deliberate practice**:
- A **specific goal** just beyond your current ability
- **Full focus**, not autopilot
- **Immediate feedback** on what went wrong
- **Repetition with adjustment** until it improves

It is usually less fun than playing for enjoyment. That is normal.

source.label: Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Romer (1993), Psychological Review

steps.tip: Before your next practice of any skill, write one specific goal on paper, like 'land 7 of 10 free throws with my elbow in.' Check it at the end.

steps.prompt: Match each practice session to what it is missing.
steps.hint: Check each session against the four parts: specific goal, full focus, feedback, repetition with adjustment.
pairs: Shooting 100 free throws while chatting, not tracking makes
Focus and feedback
Playing the songs you already know perfectly
A goal just beyond your ability
Writing essays but never reading the teacher's comments
Using feedback to adjust
Trying the hardest piece in the book with no idea how to start
A goal at the right level (too far beyond you)
steps.explain: Deliberate practice needs all four parts: a stretch goal at the right level, full attention, feedback, and adjustment.

steps.title: What about 10,000 hours?
steps.body:
The '10,000-hour rule' became famous from popular books, but it oversimplifies the research.

A 2014 analysis of many studies found practice clearly matters, but it explained only part of the differences in skill: about a quarter in games, about a fifth in music, less in sports, and very little in school and professions. Starting age, coaching quality, and other factors also count.

> Practice is the part you control. The **quality** of your practice matters as much as the hours.
steps.tip: Ask a coach, teacher or skilled friend for five minutes of feedback on one thing you do. One good correction can beat hours of practice alone.

source.label: Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald (2014), Psychological Science

steps.prompt: Research shows that anyone who practices any skill for exactly 10,000 hours will reach expert level.
steps.explain: There is no magic number. Practice amounts vary a lot among experts, practice explains only part of skill differences, and the kind of practice matters greatly.

steps.prompt: You have played guitar for a year and feel stuck. You practice 30 minutes a day, mostly playing songs you already know. What change will help most?

options.text: Spend 20 of the 30 minutes on one weak spot (like a fast chord change), playing it slowly with a metronome, recording yourself and speeding up only when it's clean. Keep 10 minutes for fun songs.
options.feedback: This targets a specific weakness, adds feedback through the recording and metronome, and keeps some enjoyment so you stick with it.

options.text: Practice for 2 hours a day the same way.
options.feedback: More of the same autopilot practice mostly builds the same level of skill. Change the type of practice first.

options.text: Buy a better guitar.
options.feedback: Gear rarely fixes a practice problem.

options.text: Learn 10 new songs at once to push yourself.
options.feedback: Breadth can be fun, but trying everything at once spreads focus thin. Pick the specific skill holding you back.

steps.explain: Find the specific weak spot, practice it slowly with full focus and feedback, and increase difficulty step by step.

steps.title: Slow is smooth, smooth is fast
steps.body:
When you practice a hard part at full speed, you often repeat your mistakes. A better loop:

1. Slow it down until you can do it correctly.
2. Repeat it correctly a few times.
3. Speed up a little.
4. When errors appear, slow back down.

This works for music, typing, sports moves, coding drills, even speaking a new language.
steps.tip: Use a metronome app or a video playback speed setting to practice a hard part at 70% speed. Speed up only once you get it right three times in a row.

steps.prompt: Order a deliberate practice session for a hard skill.
items: Pick one specific weakness to work on
Do it slowly enough to get it right
Get feedback (recording, coach, answer key, timer)
Adjust and repeat correctly several times
Increase speed or difficulty slightly
steps.explain: Target, slow down, measure, fix, then push a little further. Then repeat the loop next session.

steps.prompt: Which practice session is closest to deliberate practice for learning to type faster?
options: Chatting online for an hour
Typing test drills on the 10 words you most often mistype, tracking accuracy, speeding up only at 95%+ accuracy
Typing the same paragraph you know by heart as fast as you can
Watching videos of fast typists
steps.explain: It targets specific weaknesses, measures accuracy, and raises difficulty only when ready. The others are either autopilot, already mastered, or passive.

steps.prompt: Name one skill you want to improve. What is one specific weakness, and how will you practice it with feedback for 15 minutes this week?
steps.placeholder: e.g. Basketball: left-hand layups, 15 min Wed with a friend filming...

levels.title: Feedback Loops and Explaining
levels.summary: Plan a new skill, get feedback fast, and use explaining to find gaps.

steps.title: The fastest learners get feedback fastest
steps.body:
A **feedback loop** is: try, see the result, adjust, try again. The shorter the loop, the faster you learn.

- Learning to cook: you taste right away. Fast loop.
- Writing essays: the grade comes back in two weeks. Slow loop.

You can shorten slow loops: check answer keys right after each problem, ask a friend to read one paragraph today, record yourself speaking and listen back, or use a coach for five minutes instead of waiting for the final review.
steps.tip: When you do homework with an answer key, check after every problem, not after the whole set, so you catch a wrong method before you repeat it.

steps.prompt: You are learning to code by building a small website. Which habit shortens your feedback loop the most?
options: Writing the whole site, then running it once at the end
Running and checking the page after each small change
Reading three coding books before writing any code
Waiting for a friend to review the finished project next month
steps.explain: Testing after each small change shows you immediately what broke and why. Writing everything first means hunting for many errors at once.

steps.title: Explain it simply
steps.body:
One of the best ways to find gaps is to **explain an idea in plain words**, as if to a 12-year-old. Researchers call related techniques **self-explanation** and **elaborative interrogation** (asking 'why is this true?'). Both were rated moderately useful in the 2013 review.

The method:
1. Write the topic at the top of a page.
2. Explain it simply, with an example.
3. Where you get stuck or use jargon, you found a gap. Go back to the source.
4. Simplify again.

This is often called the Feynman technique, after the physicist who explained things this way.

source.label: Dunlosky et al. (2013), Psychological Science in the Public Interest

steps.tip: Pick one idea from class today and explain it out loud to a family member at dinner in under a minute. Wherever you stumble is what to review.

steps.prompt: Put the explain-it-simply method in order.
items: Pick a concept and write its name at the top of a page
Explain it in plain words with an example, without notes
Mark the spots where you got stuck or used jargon
Go back to your notes or source to fill those gaps
Explain it again, more simply
steps.explain: The point is not a perfect explanation on the first try. It is finding exactly where your understanding breaks.

steps.prompt: You want to learn to cook five basic dinners in a month. Which plan has the best feedback loop?

options.text: Cook one recipe twice a week, taste as you go, ask your family for one thing to improve, and note changes on the recipe card.
options.feedback: Frequent attempts, instant taste feedback, outside feedback, and notes to adjust next time. That is a tight loop.

options.text: Watch 20 hours of cooking shows first, then try all five recipes in one weekend.
options.feedback: Watching is passive, and cooking everything at once gives little time to adjust between tries.

options.text: Cook each recipe once and move on, even if it didn't turn out.
options.feedback: No repetition, so the lesson from each attempt is never used.

options.text: Only cook when guests come over so it's worth the effort.
options.feedback: Rare attempts mean slow learning, and high-pressure settings make mistakes more stressful.

steps.explain: Try often, get immediate and outside feedback, write down the adjustment, and repeat soon.

steps.title: A plan for any new skill
steps.body:
1. **Define success:** 'Hold a 5-minute conversation in Spanish' beats 'learn Spanish.'
2. **Break it down:** list the sub-skills and start with the ones you use most.
3. **Learn just enough** to start practicing, then practice.
4. **Remove barriers:** put the guitar on a stand, not in its case.
5. **Get feedback early and often.**
6. **Practice a little most days** rather than one marathon a week.
steps.tip: Pick one skill you want this month and write a one-line success goal, like 'cook three dinners on my own.' Put your first 20-minute practice in your calendar.

steps.prompt: When learning a new skill, it is best to read and watch everything about it before you start practicing, so you don't build bad habits.
steps.explain: Some instruction first is helpful, but long study before trying delays feedback. Learn just enough to begin, practice, and let your mistakes show you what to study next.

steps.prompt: Which of these shorten a slow feedback loop? Select all that apply.
options: Checking the answer key after each practice problem
Recording a practice speech and watching it the same day
Waiting for the end-of-term grade to see how you did
Asking a friend to read just your intro paragraph today
Avoiding practice tests so you don't feel discouraged
steps.explain: Answer keys, recordings and quick partial reviews give feedback within minutes or hours. Waiting for the term grade or avoiding tests keeps you in the dark.

steps.prompt: Pick a skill you want to start this month. Write your success definition, the first sub-skill, and how you will get feedback this week.

levels.title: Sleep: Your Brain's Save Button
levels.summary: How sleep locks in memories and why all-nighters backfire.

steps.title: Learning continues while you sleep
steps.body:
During sleep, your brain replays and reorganizes what you learned during the day, moving it into more lasting storage. This is called **memory consolidation**.

Sleep also prepares your brain to learn the next day. In a 2007 study, young adults who stayed awake all night were much worse at forming new memories the next day than people who slept, and brain scans showed less activity in the hippocampus, a key memory area.
steps.tip: Do a short self-quiz on the hardest material in the evening, then go to bed on time. Sleep strengthens what you just practiced.

steps.prompt: Pulling an all-nighter before an exam is a good trade, because the extra hours of study outweigh the lost sleep.
steps.explain: Losing a night of sleep hurts attention and the ability to recall and form memories the next day. The extra hours rarely make up for it, especially compared with studying earlier and sleeping.

steps.title: How much do you need?
steps.body:
Sleep medicine experts in the US recommend:
- **Ages 13-18:** 8 to 10 hours a night
- **Adults 18+:** 7 or more hours

Many teens get far less, partly because their body clocks naturally shift later. That makes a consistent schedule even more important.

Signs you are short on sleep: needing an alarm to drag you out every day, falling asleep in class, and sleeping much longer on weekends.
steps.tip: Set a phone bedtime reminder that goes off 30 minutes before you need to be in bed, so you start winding down on time.

source.label: American Academy of Sleep Medicine (2016), pediatric consensus statement, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine

steps.prompt: You need to wake up at 6:30 a.m. You want 9 hours of sleep, and it usually takes you about 15 minutes to fall asleep. You should get into bed at 9:__ p.m. What number goes in the blank?
steps.hint: First count back 9 hours from 6:30 a.m. to find when you need to be asleep. Then go earlier by the time it takes to fall asleep.
steps.explain: Count back 9 hours from 6:30 a.m.: that is 9:30 p.m., when you want to be asleep. Take off 15 minutes to fall asleep, and you should be in bed at 9:15 p.m.

steps.prompt: It is 11:30 p.m. the night before a big test. You have studied for 2 hours but feel you could do 2 more. You need to wake at 6:30. What is the best choice?
steps.hint: Weigh two more hours of tired studying against what sleep does for memory and focus during the test.

options.text: Do a quick 10-minute self-quiz on the hardest topics, then go to sleep, and review those flashcards once over breakfast.
options.feedback: You get one more retrieval round, protect about 7 hours of sleep, and do a short morning review. Good balance.

options.text: Study until 1:30 a.m., then sleep 5 hours.
options.feedback: Two more hours at midnight, tired, add less than you think, and short sleep hurts recall and focus during the test.

options.text: Drink an energy drink and stay up all night.
options.feedback: This is the riskiest option: no consolidation, poor attention, and the crash may hit during the test.

options.text: Go to bed but keep reviewing notes on your phone in bed for an hour.
options.feedback: This cuts sleep and screen use in bed can delay falling asleep. If you want a last review, do it before bed, briefly.

steps.explain: Near the end, sleep is worth more than extra late-night hours. Better still: next time start a few days earlier so the night before is short.

steps.title: Sleep habits that help
steps.body:
- **Same wake time** most days, including weekends (within about an hour).
- **Phone out of bed:** charge it across the room. Use a cheap alarm clock if needed.
- **Wind down** 30 minutes before bed: dim lights, no intense games or scrolling.
- **Caffeine:** avoid it after early afternoon; it lasts for hours. In one study, a large dose taken even 6 hours before bed still disrupted sleep.
- **Short naps** (20-30 minutes, no later than about 3-4 p.m.) can help; long late naps can wreck the night.
- **Study, then sleep:** reviewing in the evening and sleeping on it is a great combo.
steps.tip: Tonight, plug your phone in to charge across the room instead of next to your bed. Use a cheap alarm clock if you need one.

source.label: Drake et al. (2013), Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine

steps.prompt: Which habits are likely to improve your sleep? Select all that apply.
options: Waking up at about the same time every day
Charging your phone across the room
A large energy drink at 5 p.m. to finish homework
Sleeping until noon on Saturdays to catch up
A 20-minute nap right after school, around 3 p.m.
steps.explain: A steady wake time, a phone out of reach and a short early nap help. Late caffeine delays sleep, and very long weekend sleep-ins shift your body clock, making Monday mornings harder.

steps.prompt: Final challenge: plan your next 2 weeks of learning for one subject or skill. Include self-testing, spaced review days, one mixed practice session, a focus setup and your bedtime.
steps.placeholder: Subject: ... Review days: ... Mixed practice: ... Focus block time: ... Bedtime: ...
